summary: Joan Fletcher, PCC, a leadership coach, argues in this LinkedIn article that body language is central to emotional intelligence (EQ) at work. She cites Albert Mehrabian's claim that most communication is nonverbal, maps the four EQ elements onto body language, and lists common workplace body-language cues for confident, nervous, defensive, bored and thinking states. Reader comments challenge the Mehrabian figures as a misinterpreted urban legend and question whether little eye contact always signals boredom.
one_line: Joan Fletcher's LinkedIn article links body language to emotional intelligence and lists common workplace nonverbal cues, with reader pushback on Mehrabian's statistics.
key_facts: Joan Fletcher, PCC, is author and founder of The Leadership Evolution Program and CEO and President of Winning Ways Inc.
The article was published on June 30, 2015.
Fletcher states that in some studies 93% of daily communication is nonverbal.
Dr. Albert Mehrabian found that 7% of any message is conveyed through words.
Dr. Albert Mehrabian found that 38% of a message is conveyed through certain vocal elements.
Dr. Albert Mehrabian found that 55% of a message is conveyed through nonverbal elements such as facial expressions, gestures and posture.
The article defines emotional intelligence (EQ) as the sum of four parts: self-awareness, self-management, social awareness and relationship management.
Under the EQ framework, self-management means paying attention to and mitigating changes in body language as the situation changes.
The article lists five workplace body-language states: confident, nervous or uncertain, defensive, bored and not paying attention, and thinking before responding.
For the confident state, the article lists solid eye contact, a relaxed face, flowing wide hand movements, open arms, walking with purpose and a firm handshake.
For the defensive state, the article lists little to no eye contact, arms crossed over the chest, small hand gestures close to the body, a mostly neutral face and the body turned away.
A commenter, Rosamina Lowi, wrote that Dr. Mehrabian's two 1967 studies had serious methodological limitations and that he said his results were misinterpreted.
A commenter, Darren Scher, questioned whether little or no eye contact necessarily means bored or not paying attention, referring to the DISC model.
The article had 18 likes and 7 comments at the time of capture.
